hints: Hint 1: Look closely at Y and Z. Y has concentrated sucrose solution and Z has dilute sucrose solution, so ask yourself where water will enter by osmosis most strongly.
Hint 2: Remember that water entry builds up high hydrostatic pressure. In a plant, flow in phloem is always from high pressure at the source (leaves) to low pressure at the sink (roots).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Observe what the model shows**
Think of this like two tiny plant cells sitting in water. Y is full of concentrated sucrose, Z is full of dilute sucrose. Both are surrounded by a partially permeable membrane.

Water will move into both by osmosis, but much more water will enter Y because its water potential is lower.

Step 2: **Work out the pressure and flow**
More water entering Y means higher hydrostatic (turgor) pressure builds up at Y than at Z. This pressure pushes sucrose solution up and along the top tube W, from high pressure to low pressure.

So flow along W is from Y to Z.

Step 3: **Map the model onto the real plant**
The top tube carrying sucrose solution, W, is the phloem sieve tube. The bottom tube carrying water back, X, is the xylem.

Y with high sucrose is the source, the leaves where sucrose is loaded. Z with low sucrose is the sink, the roots where sucrose is used or stored. That matches option B perfectly.

options.A: W as phloem and X as xylem is correct, but Y cannot be roots. Y has concentrated sucrose so it must be the source (leaves), and flow cannot be from Z to Y.
options.B: W is phloem, X is xylem, Y is leaves (source, high sucrose and high pressure) and Z is roots (sink, low sucrose). Flow along W is correctly from Y to Z.
options.C: X cannot be phloem. X is the lower tube carrying only water back, so it is xylem. W carrying sucrose solution is phloem.
options.D: W is phloem not xylem, and flow is from high pressure (Y, leaves) to low pressure (Z, roots), not from Z to Y.
